The Blackside darter (Percina maculata) reaches a maximum recorded body size of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters] in total length, a relatively modest dimension typical of small-bodied benthic predators in the subgenus Hadropterus. Comparative studies within the Etheostomatinae indicate that this ultimate length aligns closely with body size constraints imposed by riffle-dwelling life in moderate-gradient streams of the Mississippi and Ohio River drainages. Mature females typically attain this length by their third or fourth growing season, after which somatic growth slows considerably. Juvenile darters exhibit rapid linear growth during their first summer, with standard length at the onset of gonadal activation—marking the transition to reproductive maturity—measured at 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters]. This standard length at puberty is consistent with the minimum size threshold observed among percid fishes for successful vitellogenesis and spermiation, reflecting a critical body size that balances the energetic demands of gamete production against the risks of delayed reproduction in an unpredictable floodplain environment.

Field collections during the spring spawning period from streams in central Illinois revealed that gravid female Blackside darters deposited adhesive eggs over gravel substrates at water temperatures that averaged 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive output was characterized by an annual fecundity of approximately 1785 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1785 eggs per year], a rate derived from a single spawning event per breeding season that deposits demersal ova in well-oxygenated interstitial spaces. This annual reproductive strategy positions Percina maculata among the iteroparous lithophils that synchronize a single spawn with the spring rise in discharge to maximize offspring survival. The hatchlings emerge at a wet weight at birth of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value derived from the dimensions of the oil-globule-laden eggs that average 1.3 millimeters in diameter. This minute mass at eclosion constrains early larval dispersal distances.

Throughout the larval period, the free-swimming prolarvae experience rapid dry mass gain while relying on endogenous yolk reserves and, after the onset of exogenous feeding, on a diet of microcrustaceans. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adult Blackside darters reaches 9.5 grams [Wwi = 9.5 grams], a value that correlates strongly with the 11-centimeter ultimate total length through a length-weight relationship whose exponent approximates 3.14. This asymptotic mass is attained during the early portion of the reproductive life span and represents a trade-off between the allocation of surplus energy to gonadal development and the maintenance of lipid reserves necessary to overwinter successfully. In contrast to larger-bodied percids such as Sander vitreus, the relatively low asymptotic mass of Percina maculata reflects its specialization as a benthic invertebrate feeder that targets chironomid larvae and ephemeropteran nymphs in shallow swift-water microhabitats where energetic acquisition rates are moderate.

Estimates of maximum longevity derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in stable, groundwater-fed headwater streams in southern Indiana at a mean annual temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] indicate that the species persists for approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days]. This lifespan of about five years is typical for a small darter inhabiting thermally constant spring-influenced environments, where the absence of severe winter hypoxia reduces the physiological costs associated with seasonal temperature extremes. Scale annulus readings from senescent individuals captured during early autumn frequently show compressed inter-annular distances during the final year of life, signaling a period of reproductive senescence and diminished foraging activity. The last spawning event often occurs during the late spring preceding natural mortality, with post-reproductive females frequently exhibiting signs of physiological deterioration consistent with age-related organ failure.

Comparisons with the congener Percina caprodes, which commonly shares riffle habitats across the central United States, highlight that Blackside darter matures at a smaller standard length at puberty of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters] but exhibits a comparable suite of life-history attributes. Egg diameter measurements from freshly spawned clutches collected in field conditions confirm the mean oocyte size of 1.3 millimeters that underlies the wet weight at birth of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], and the resulting free-swimming larva at first exogenous feeding is among the smallest pelagic ichthyoplankton produced within the genus. The interplay between the moderate ultimate total length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters] and the 13 °C [T = 13 °C] thermal regime that governs both reproductive rate and longevity shapes a life-history strategy characterized by relatively late maturation, a single annual spawning episode, and a maximum lifespan of approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days] in its natural lotic environment.
